claims.text: Pulumi's component state migrations let component authors ship an upgrade path with the component; a migration translates the saved state of a component and its children before Pulumi works out which resources need to change.
Pulumi component state migrations are a new feature.
The Pulumi component state migrations API is experimental and may change.
Replacing a VPC forces replacement of the security group that refers to the VPC's ID (per AWS CloudFormation EC2 SecurityGroup VpcId docs).
The v1 example uses the legacy `awsx.classic.ec2.Vpc` component, creating a VPC with one isolated subnet, a route table and association, and an internet gateway.
A replacement database does not automatically contain the old database's data.

Legacy AWSX wraps the subnet and internet gateway in separate components; modern AWSX removes those wrappers; the subnet's Pulumi name changes from `vpc-isolated-0` to `vpc-isolated-1` in the example.
Each record in Pulumi state has a Pulumi name called a URN, and managed resources also have a provider ID.
Pulumi aliases handle changes to a resource's name, type, or parent when its saved state remains compatible, but do not remove component wrappers or transfer references.
Pulumi resource options accept a `stateMigrations` option taking a migration callback, used together with an alias for the legacy component type.

A state migration callback receives the aliased component's saved state followed by its children's state, and returns `newState` (complete replacement records) and `successors` (map from each disappearing old URN to its replacement URN).
Pulumi uses successors mappings to update dependencies and resource references elsewhere in the stack, keeping the security group's VPC reference valid.

Pulumi runs multiple state migration callbacks in order, passing each result to the next; a stack on legacy AWSX can upgrade directly to plain AWS; a stack on modern AWSX skips the first migration; completed migrations return no result on later updates.
After a migration, Pulumi compares the new program with the migrated state and calls the provider for remaining changes; the example can still show in-place updates for provider defaults and tags.
`pulumi preview` evaluates the state migration without saving it, and `pulumi up` saves the migrated state.
When users upgrade a component that registers a migration, Pulumi runs the migration automatically as part of normal preview and update, without users writing the migration or editing stack state.
A component state migrations guide exists at /docs/iac/guides/building-extending/components/state-migrations/ covering the callback contract.
The pulumi/examples repo contains aws-ts-awsx-vpc-state-migration with v1, v2, v3 programs and migration code (v2/migration.ts, v3/migration.ts).
A component state migrations discussion exists at github.com/pulumi/pulumi/discussions/24799.
State migration callbacks (the stateMigrations resource option) run during previews and updates when prior state exists.
State migration callbacks must be idempotent and return no result when the state no longer needs migration.
State migration callbacks rewrite state without performing provider operations.
A Pulumi component state migration is a pure function that transforms the saved state of a component and its children into the state expected by a new component version.
A component state migration callback returns the updated state records and successor mappings.
Each successor mapping in a component state migration result connects an old URN omitted from the result to the URN of the returned resource that takes its place.
If no migration is needed, a component state migration callback returns no result.
A component state migration callback that returns no result can remain attached when using update plans or targeted updates.
The restrictions on state-changing results of component state migrations do not require removing an already-applied migration when using update plans or targeted updates.
Pulumi component state migration entries use the checkpoint resource format, including fields such as urn, type, id, parent, provider, inputs, and outputs.
